text: You have been asked to contribute to a company's internal magazine. Which role would you take?

text: A popular saying goes: 'Form follows function.' Do you agree?
options: A) Disagree - beauty and aesthetic quality have intrinsic value beyond function
B) Agree - practicality and usability should always come before how something looks

text: Your team needs to communicate a complex strategy to a non-technical audience. Which approach do you instinctively prefer?
options: A) Craft a compelling narrative with visuals and metaphors that make it memorable and emotionally resonant
B) Build a clear logical argument with evidence, data, and structured reasoning
C) Create an interactive presentation where the audience participates and co-discovers the insight
D) Develop a detailed written document with precise language, definitions, and references

text: You are reading two competing explanations for the same historical event. What do you naturally do?
options: A) Try to evaluate the evidence behind each and figure out which is more credible
B) Accept the one that came from the more authoritative source
C) Find the most interesting narrative and go with that
D) Share both with a friend and see what they think

text: A researcher role becomes available that requires spending 70% of your time reading academic literature and synthesising findings. How do you feel?
options: A) This sounds genuinely appealing - deep reading and synthesis is work I find absorbing
B) This sounds tedious - I prefer applying knowledge rather than accumulating it

text: Rank the following from most to least likely to occupy your thoughts during a long commute.
options: A) A complex question about how something in the world actually works
B) A creative project you are working on or want to start
C) An interesting person you met recently and what makes them tick
D) A challenge at work and how to navigate it more effectively

text: Your school is starting a peer counselling programme where trained students support classmates going through stress, family issues, or academic pressure. Would you volunteer?
options: A) Yes enthusiastically - this is exactly the kind of meaningful role I find fulfilling
B) Yes, if I could receive proper training first - I want to help but need to feel prepared
C) Probably not - I care about people but find it hard to handle others' emotional weight
D) No - I prefer supporting friends informally rather than in a structured role

text: Which type of professional impact would feel most meaningful to you personally, if everything else were equal?
options: A) Changing one person's life trajectory profoundly and permanently
B) Improving the lives of thousands of people in a smaller but measurable way

text: Your college asks you to represent them at a regional competition where you need to pitch a new idea and persuade a panel of judges. How do you feel?
options: A) Excited - pitching and persuading are among the activities I enjoy most
B) Willing but nervous - I would need preparation and practice to feel comfortable
C) Reluctant - public persuasion does not come naturally to me
D) Strongly prefer not to - this type of high-stakes presentation is very stressful for me

text: A colleague describes their dream as becoming the best specialist in their field - the go-to expert everyone calls. Another colleague's dream is to build and lead an organisation. Whose ambition resonates more with you?
options: A) The specialist - deep domain mastery is what I aspire to
B) The organisational builder - I want to lead and create something larger than myself

text: How do you feel when a project you are working on has no clear milestones, no deadlines, and no defined deliverables?
options: A) Uncomfortable - I work best when there is a clear structure and timeline to organise against
B) Mixed - I can adapt, but I would create my own structure to stay on track
C) Fine - open-ended projects give me flexibility to explore and be creative
D) Energising - the absence of constraints lets me think and work more freely

text: You are handed a large dataset of company expenses with inconsistencies, missing entries, and formatting errors. What is your reaction?
options: A) This is satisfying work - cleaning and organising data carefully is something I enjoy
B) Manageable, but I would want to do it methodically to avoid introducing new errors
C) Tedious - I would rather hand this to someone who enjoys detail work
D) Frustrating - messy, unstructured data makes it hard for me to think clearly

text: You have two weekend project options. Option A: Restore an old bicycle - disassemble, clean, repair, and reassemble. Option B: Write a long-form analytical essay on a topic you know well. Which excites you more?
options: A) Option A - hands-on, tangible work with a physical outcome appeals to me
B) Option B - intellectual, written work suits my natural inclinations better

text: When you hear about someone who builds things with their hands for a living - a carpenter, a mechatronics engineer, a civil contractor - what is your honest reaction?
options: A) Genuine admiration and envy - I find that kind of tangible, skilled physical work deeply appealing
B) Respect - it is clearly skilled and valuable work, though not for me
C) Neutral - it is a job like any other
D) I would find that kind of work unfulfilling compared to more intellectual or people-focused careers

text: Your school offers a new activity: building a fully functional robot from components using a technical manual. Would you sign up?
options: A) Definitely - this kind of hands-on technical building is exactly what I love
B) Probably - it sounds interesting and I would like to try it
C) Maybe - depends on whether there is a good teacher and whether it counts for something
D) Unlikely - I prefer activities that involve reading, writing, or working with people

text: Your internship placement is at a design consultancy. Most of your work will involve generating concepts, exploring visual directions, and experimenting without a guaranteed outcome. How do you feel?
options: A) Excited - open-ended creative exploration is where I do my best work
B) Cautiously optimistic - I can work creatively but prefer some constraints or direction
C) Uncertain - I am not sure I have the creative confidence for open-ended design work
D) Uncomfortable - I prefer roles with clearer deliverables and evaluation criteria

text: You have the opportunity to spend 20% of your work time mentoring junior colleagues, with no additional pay. Would you take it?
options: A) Yes eagerly - developing others is one of the most fulfilling parts of work
B) Yes, but I would want to be thoughtful about time commitment and impact
C) Probably not - I care about people but the opportunity cost is high
D) No - I prefer to invest my time in my own work and development

text: You are listening to a debate and one speaker makes a point that sounds persuasive but something feels off. What do you do?
options: A) Mentally trace the argument to identify where the reasoning breaks down
B) Note the doubt but continue listening - I may have missed something
C) Accept the argument if others in the room seem convinced
D) Raise my concern immediately without fully articulating the flaw

text: You are reviewing a business proposal. The financial projections look attractive but rest on several assumptions. What do you focus on first?
options: A) Challenge the assumptions - the projections are only as good as what they rest on
B) Focus on the opportunity size and strategic fit - details can be stress-tested later

text: How naturally do you notice inconsistencies or contradictions when reading a document, watching a presentation, or listening to an argument?
options: 1 = Rarely, if ever
2 = Sometimes, if they are obvious
3 = Often
4 = Very often - I notice most inconsistencies
5 = Almost always - it is one of my most natural cognitive habits

text: You are planning a team event and need to balance a tight budget across venue, food, and activities. How do you approach this?
options: A) Build a simple spreadsheet or mental model to optimise allocation across the three categories
B) Make reasonable estimates and adjust on the day based on what is needed
C) Ask someone more comfortable with numbers to manage the budget
D) Keep it simple and just allocate equal thirds to each category

text: You need to estimate the market size of a new product category in India, with no data immediately available. What do you do?
options: A) Use first-principles estimation - build up from population, penetration rates, and average spend
B) Research to find any proxies, comparable markets, or published data before estimating
C) Acknowledge I cannot estimate this reliably without better data
D) Give a rough order-of-magnitude guess and flag the high uncertainty

text: How comfortable are you mentally calculating rough percentages, proportions, or growth rates in real time without a calculator?
options: 1 = Not at all comfortable
2 = Somewhat uncomfortable
3 = Neutral
4 = Comfortable
5 = Very comfortable - I do this naturally and quickly

text: You are asked to chair a panel discussion at a college event on a topic you know moderately well. How do you feel?
options: A) Confident - facilitating discussions and thinking on my feet verbally is a strength
B) Capable - I can do it well with some preparation
C) Nervous - I struggle to think and articulate clearly under public pressure
D) Strongly prefer not to - verbal performance in front of groups is not my strength

text: A friend reads your written work and says: 'Your arguments are solid, but the writing feels flat - it doesn't pull you in.' How do you typically respond to this kind of feedback?
options: A) I take it seriously and work on making my writing more engaging and vivid
B) I appreciate the feedback but am not sure how to address the 'flat' quality
C) I accept it - I prioritise clarity and logic over stylistic flair
D) I disagree - in professional contexts, clear logic matters more than engaging prose

text: How much do you enjoy the craft of writing - choosing the right word, structuring a sentence for rhythm, or shaping a paragraph for impact?
options: 1 = Not at all - writing is purely functional for me
2 = A little
3 = Somewhat
4 = Quite a lot
5 = Very much - the craft of language genuinely excites me

text: You are tasked with naming a new product. You have one hour to generate options. What do you produce?
options: A) A large, eclectic list with wild ideas, puns, metaphors, and unexpected angles - I throw everything at the wall
B) A focused list of five to eight strong, well-reasoned names that fit the brief
C) A few solid options after careful thought about what would work in the market
D) I struggle with this kind of generative task - I would prefer to evaluate others' ideas

text: Your organisation is doing the same thing the same way it has done for years. You are asked to diagnose why and propose alternatives. What is your natural first move?
options: A) Challenge every assumption about why things are done this way - question the fundamentals before proposing anything
B) Research how other organisations tackle the same challenge before proposing anything
C) Map the current process carefully to understand the problem before jumping to solutions
D) Convene stakeholders and use their combined knowledge to identify what needs to change

text: You are asked to describe verbally to someone how to get from Point A to Point B in a city you know well, without using a map. How easy do you find this?
options: A) Easy - I hold a strong mental map and can translate it into clear verbal directions
B) Manageable - I can do it but need to think carefully and may miss a detail
C) Difficult - I navigate by feel and landmarks rather than a systematic spatial model
D) Very difficult - I rely heavily on navigation apps and could not reliably give verbal directions

text: You are designing the layout for a physical retail space - traffic flow, product placement, signage positioning. How do you approach this?
options: A) I can visualise the space and mentally walk through multiple configurations before settling on one
B) I would need to physically sketch it out or walk the empty space to think through the options

text: You spend three months on a project and it turns out exactly as planned - solid, competent, nothing exceptional. How do you feel?
options: A) Quietly disappointed - I was hoping to produce something more exceptional
B) Satisfied - delivering well against a plan is a success
C) Fine - not every project needs to be exceptional and I move on
D) Relieved - meeting expectations without drama is a good outcome

text: How much does external recognition - awards, titles, rankings, public acknowledgment - matter to you as a motivator?
options: 1 = Not at all - I am internally motivated and recognition does not move me
2 = Slightly
3 = Moderately
4 = Significantly
5 = A great deal - recognition is a primary driver for me

text: You are about to submit a project you are proud of. A peer glances at it and says it is 'good enough - just send it.' How do you respond?
options: A) Push back - good enough is not good enough if I know it can be better
B) Take a breath and honestly assess whether my perfectionism is holding me back
C) Trust their read - external perspective on readiness is often more objective than mine
D) Send it - I have a tendency to over-invest and this is a reasonable checkpoint

text: Your college gives you a free elective slot with no guidance on what to take. You can take anything. How do you feel about this freedom?
options: A) Excited - I love having the ability to choose something driven entirely by my own curiosity
B) Pleased but slightly anxious - the freedom is good but I would appreciate some guidance
C) Mildly overwhelmed - too many options makes decision-making harder for me
D) I would ask a teacher or advisor for a recommendation and follow that

text: Which of these two career arcs appeals to you more over a 20-year horizon?
options: A) Progressive independence - starting with more direction and earning increasing ownership over time
B) Structured advancement - a clear ladder with defined roles, milestones, and rewards at each level

text: Your organisation offers a sabbatical - three months of paid leave to do whatever you want. What do you do with it?
options: A) Rest, travel, and invest in personal relationships - I want to fully recharge
B) Pursue a creative or personal project I have never had time for
C) Learn a new skill or take a course that would accelerate my professional development
D) Honestly - I would probably still do some work and check in regularly

text: A senior leader at your firm is described as brilliant but famously difficult to work with - short temper, unreasonable hours, takes credit from the team. Would you work for them to access the career opportunity?
options: A) Yes - learning from the best, even under difficult conditions, is worth it for a defined period
B) Yes, but I would set firm personal boundaries from day one
C) Only if I had no other comparable path to the opportunity
D) No - working conditions and personal wellbeing are non-negotiable for me

text: You are evaluating two long-term career outcomes: Career A offers Rs 1 crore/year in 10 years but requires navigating high uncertainty and possible failure along the way. Career B offers Rs 40 LPA in 10 years with a near-certain, predictable path. Which do you choose?
options: A) Career A - the upside justifies the uncertainty and I am willing to navigate the risk
B) Career B - a reliable, predictable outcome is more valuable to me than the upside of Career A

text: Your family asks if you would consider a government job after graduation for the security it offers. How do you honestly feel about this suggestion?
options: A) Open to it - job security and stability are genuinely important factors for me
B) Neutral - I would consider it only if the work itself was meaningful
C) Unlikely - I want more dynamic, high-growth opportunities
D) Firmly no - the pace and structure of government work does not align with how I want to work

text: You read that a technology you helped build is being used in ways that harm marginalised communities, even though those uses were not intended. What is your reaction?
options: A) I feel responsible and would actively push to address the harm - even at personal cost
B) I feel concern and would raise it internally through appropriate channels
C) I feel bad but see it as beyond my individual control - these are systemic problems
D) I would focus on my own work and trust that others responsible will address it

text: A friend says: 'Career is career and charity is charity - trying to combine them usually means doing both badly.' How do you respond?
options: A) I disagree - the best careers are ones that create value for society and for yourself simultaneously
B) I partially agree - most attempts to do both usually compromise one or the other

text: At what point does more money stop being a meaningful motivator for you?
options: A) When I have built significant financial independence - I want real wealth, not just comfort
B) When I have enough to live comfortably without financial worry
C) When basic needs and some lifestyle quality are covered
D) Money has never been a strong motivator beyond providing security

text: You receive an unexpected bonus of Rs 5 lakhs. What is your most instinctive response?
options: A) Invest it aggressively - I want it to grow as part of building long-term wealth
B) Save a portion, invest a portion, and spend a small part on something meaningful
C) Use it for something that would significantly improve my current quality of life
D) Set it aside as a financial buffer - security matters more than growth

text: Which of the following statements about money resonates most deeply with how you actually live and think?
options: A) Money is freedom - having a lot of it means never having to compromise on what you want to do
B) Money is security - enough of it means you and your family are protected from the worst outcomes
C) Money is a tool - it enables experiences and choices but is not an end in itself
D) Money is overrated - the most meaningful things in life cannot be bought

text: You are leading a team through a difficult period - poor morale, unclear direction, and underperformance. What do you do first?
options: A) Clarify the direction and reconnect the team to purpose - people need to know why before they commit to how
B) Identify the specific performance gaps and have direct conversations about what needs to change
C) Build individual relationships - understand each person's frustration before addressing the group
D) Escalate to senior leadership and ask for more clarity or resources before making moves

text: How do you feel about being the person ultimately accountable for an outcome - where the success or failure rests clearly with you?
options: 1 = Very uncomfortable - I prefer shared accountability
2 = Somewhat uncomfortable
3 = Neutral
4 = Comfortable
5 = Energising - individual accountability is when I do my best work

text: Your team's morale is low after a setback. You are not the formal leader. What do you do?
options: A) Informally step into a supportive role - talk to individuals, rally energy, and help reset the mood
B) Leave it to the designated leader - it is not my place to step into that role unbidden

text: Which work scenario would you find most difficult to sustain over six months?
options: A) A role with a new crisis or urgent priority almost every day - reactive, fast-paced, unpredictable
B) A role with a slow, methodical pace - deep work, long timelines, minimal urgency

text: Your organisation introduces Agile sprints - two-week cycles with clearly defined deliverables and daily standups. How do you respond?
options: A) Genuinely positive - the rhythm and accountability of short cycles suits how I work best
B) Mostly fine - structured rhythms help, though I would prefer slightly longer cycles
C) Mixed - I value focused delivery windows but the daily standups feel like overhead
D) Resistant - I prefer longer, more autonomous work cycles without frequent check-ins

text: You have a reputation at work. Which of the following would you most want that reputation to be?
options: A) The person who always produces the highest-quality analytical or technical work
B) The person everyone goes to when they have a difficult people situation to navigate
C) The person who comes up with the most creative solutions
D) The person who gets things done - reliably and on time, no matter what

text: Your company reorganises and you can choose between two roles. Role A is individual contributor - deep, solo technical work. Role B is a relationship manager - building and sustaining client and stakeholder relationships. Which do you prefer?
options: A) Role A - solo deep work energises me and I prefer limited external interaction
B) Role B - sustained relationship-building is where I do my most meaningful work

text: You are given a week of completely unstructured time at work - no meetings, no deliverables, just explore. What is most likely to happen?
options: A) I would create my own agenda immediately and pursue it with focus and energy
B) I would explore loosely for a couple of days and then settle on something to dig into
C) I would feel slightly adrift and spend significant time trying to decide what to work on
D) I would find the freedom uncomfortable and would prefer to have at least some direction

text: Your manager gives you a goal but zero specification on how to achieve it. How do you feel?
options: A) Energised - I work best when I can figure out the best path myself
B) Comfortable - I will create my own structure and check in periodically
C) Uncertain - I would reach out to clarify at least some expectations
D) Anxious - I need more direction to work confidently

text: When you reflect on your most energising work experiences, which environment appears most often?
options: A) Working alone, fully focused, with minimal interruption or collaboration
B) Working with others - the energy of shared effort, debate, and mutual accountability

text: A cross-functional project requires you to coordinate with five different teams over three months. How do you feel about this?
options: A) Energised - I thrive in environments where I am connecting different people and teams
B) Fine - I can navigate cross-functional work well, though it can be draining
C) Wary - coordination overhead often gets in the way of actual work
D) Stressed - managing multiple team dynamics is not a natural strength for me

text: You are deciding between two cities to build your career. City A is your home city - familiar, comfortable, with moderate opportunity. City B is a different state with far more professional opportunity but requires starting from scratch socially and culturally. What do you do?
options: A) City B without much hesitation - professional opportunity outweighs personal comfort
B) City B after careful consideration and preparation
C) City A - stability and familiarity matter more to me than marginal professional upside
D) Depend entirely on specifics - there is no general answer that applies

text: A respected peer tells you they are leaving their stable corporate career to write a book for two years - no guaranteed income, but something they have always wanted to do. What is your honest reaction?
options: A) Admiration - this takes real courage and I genuinely understand the pull
B) Respect but concern - I hope they have enough saved and a plan for after
C) Confusion - it seems like a significant sacrifice for an uncertain outcome
D) Concern - it is an impractical decision and I would have tried to talk them out of it

text: Which best describes your relationship with uncertainty?
options: A) I am energised by uncertainty - it signals that real opportunity exists
B) I tolerate uncertainty well when the potential upside is clear
C) I manage uncertainty but it causes me meaningful stress
D) I avoid uncertainty wherever possible - it makes it hard for me to plan and feel settled

text: Looking at your closest friends or peers who work the most hours - do you feel envious, neutral, or relieved that you are not them?
options: A) Envious - they are building faster than I am and I should be working harder
B) Relieved - sustainable pace matters more to me than maximum output

text: If a manager explicitly encouraged you to leave early, take time off, and guard your personal life, how would you feel?
options: A) Grateful and relieved - this is the kind of environment I thrive in
B) Appreciative but I would still work my natural hours regardless
C) Slightly uncomfortable - I expect to work hard and this feels like low ambition
D) Conflicted - I value balance but I also worry about falling behind colleagues who do not take this seriously

text: How important is it to you that your long-term career is rooted in your home state or region?
options: 1 = Not important at all - I will go wherever opportunity takes me
2 = Slightly important
3 = Moderately important
4 = Very important
5 = Extremely important - staying close to home is non-negotiable

text: A global company wants to hire you but the role is fully based in Singapore - no option to work from India. The pay is 2.5x your current salary. What do you do?
options: A) Accept - international career experience and the financial upside make this an easy yes
B) Take time to evaluate carefully - the opportunity is real but so is the life disruption
C) Explore whether a remote arrangement is possible before deciding
D) Decline - I am not ready to relocate internationally at this stage

text: If you had to take a 12-month career break to pursue further education or a personal project, how financially prepared are you to do so?
options: A) Not at all - I need income to meet current obligations and cannot take a break
B) Possible if I planned and saved for 1–2 years before doing it
C) Manageable - I have or could build enough savings to sustain a 12-month break
D) Comfortable - this would not create meaningful financial strain

text: How much does your current financial situation constrain the career choices you are realistically able to consider?
options: 1 = Not at all - I have full financial flexibility
2 = Slightly
3 = Moderately
4 = Significantly
5 = Heavily - financial obligations are a major factor in every career decision I make

text: If your career choice made your parents proud, how much would that add to your sense of satisfaction with the decision?
options: A) A great deal - their approval and pride is deeply important to me
B) Somewhat - it would add to my satisfaction but would not be the primary factor
C) A little - I appreciate it but my own sense of rightness matters more
D) Not much - my career is my decision and their pride in it is a bonus, not a goal

text: You are assigned a new topic to learn for a project. Which first step do you most naturally take?
options: A) Find the single best book or structured course on the topic and work through it systematically
B) Search broadly - read a mix of articles, watch videos, and browse Reddit or forums for real-world perspectives
C) Ask someone who already knows the topic well to give me a rapid orientation
D) Start with the practical application and learn the theory as gaps emerge

text: How do you typically retain information you need to remember for the long term?
options: A) Active recall - testing myself repeatedly until it is deeply embedded
B) Spaced repetition - reviewing material at increasing intervals
C) Teaching or explaining it to someone else - if I can explain it, I know it
D) Using it in practice immediately - application is how I retain things

text: Your school offers two types of project assessment: Type A gives you a detailed brief with specific evaluation criteria. Type B gives you total freedom in how you define, approach, and present the project. Which do you prefer?
options: A) Type B - I do my best and most original work when I have full creative control
B) Type A - clear criteria help me understand what is expected and focus my efforts

text: How would you describe your approach to academic work - not your results, but your actual behaviour?
options: A) Consistently thorough - I work hard, prepare well, and rarely let standards slip
B) Variable - I engage deeply with topics I find interesting and minimally with those I do not
C) Efficient - I focus on what matters for the grade and do not invest more than necessary
D) Reactive - I perform best under deadline pressure and tend to work intensively close to submission

text: Looking back at your most recent year of study, what drove your academic performance the most?
options: A) Genuine interest in the material - I performed best in subjects I cared about
B) Discipline and effort - I applied consistent work regardless of interest level
C) Exam strategy and smart preparation - knowing what to prioritise made the difference
D) External pressure - I performed best when I had something to prove or someone to impress

text: Which of the following best describes how your academic strengths are distributed?
options: A) Concentrated - I am significantly stronger in quantitative and technical subjects
B) Concentrated - I am significantly stronger in language, humanities, and social sciences
C) Balanced - I perform relatively well across both quantitative and humanities subjects
D) Variable - my performance differs more by teacher and interest than by subject type

text: A subject you previously disliked has become genuinely interesting to you. What most likely caused that shift?
options: A) A great teacher who made the subject come alive and relevant
B) A real-world application or project that showed me why it matters
C) I started to understand it better - competence built interest
D) A friend who was passionate about it influenced how I saw it

text: How well do you feel you understand the actual day-to-day work of the career paths you are most seriously considering?
options: 1 = Not at all - I know the title but not what the work actually involves
2 = Slightly
